uncited: - Input: $n$ partial images (one per processor), where each partial image contains the rendered contribution for the entire volume but is logically divided into $n$ tiles.
- The final image is divided into $n$ equal-sized tiles in screen space.
- Each processor $P_i$ holds a local buffer containing the $n$ tiles it rendered.
Let $T_{i,j}$ be the tile $j$ rendered by processor $i$.
**All-to-All Exchange:** Each processor $P_i$ sends its tile $T_{i,j}$ to processor $P_j$ for all $j \neq i$.
Processor $P_i$ also retains its own tile $T_{i,i}$.
**Independent Compositing:** Once all tiles have arrived, each processor $P_j$ composites its assigned tile $T_{j,j}$ independently.
The compositing operation involves blending the incoming tiles $T_{i,j}$ (for all $i$) into the target tile $T_{j,j}$ using standard front-to-back or back-to-front volume compositing equations.
- Tile size: Typically $1/n$ of the total image area.
- **Network Congestion:** In the worst case, $n(n-1)$ messages are sent.
- **Memory Complexity:** Each processor stores $n$ tiles, so memory usage scales linearly with the number of processors relative to the tile size.
- **When to use:** Suitable for high-performance clusters with high-bandwidth networks where simplicity and low synchronization overhead are prioritized.
